cultivar: Assam-type seedling bushes and TRI clones
processing: Steamed or pan-fired to prevent oxidation, rolled (often tightly into gunpowder-style pellets or twisted into 'Young Hyson' leaf) and dried; made mostly for export, with the USA, Australia and Russia named as the main markets.
appearance_dry: Tight dark-green pellets (gunpowder) or twisted greyish-green leaf.
appearance_wet: Olive to khaki leaf, somewhat coarse.
taste_profile: Bold and brisk for a green: toasty, lightly nutty and vegetal with a pronounced drying finish; made for sweet mint tea rather than solo sipping.

brewing.notes: Alone, keep it cool and short; or brew it strong with fresh mint and sugar, Moroccan style.

vintage_note: Sold through the Colombo auction by grade (Gunpowder, Young Hyson, Chun Mee, Sowmee, GP Special) with no vintage marketing, plus a few estate lots under their own name; buy the current year's lot and use it within the year, as the greens stale faster than the island's black teas.
description:
Ceylon green tea is Sri Lanka's smaller, less famous green line, made by a small number of factories mostly for export, with the USA, Australia and Russia named as its main markets. It is a bold, toasty green rather than a delicate one, and the gunpowder grades suit a sweet glass of mint tea.

The leaf is steamed or pan-fired to stop oxidation, then rolled, often tightly into gunpowder-style pellets, or twisted into 'Young Hyson' leaf, and dried. Assam-type leaf makes a stronger, more astringent green than Chinese bushes.

Brewed on its own the cup is yellow to pale amber-green, toasty, nutty and vegetal with a pronounced drying finish. Keep the water around 80 °C and the steeps short, or brew it strong, add fresh mint and sugar, and pour it from a height.

It is sold by grade (Gunpowder, Young Hyson, Chun Mee, Sowmee, GP Special) with no vintage marketing, and a few estates sell small lots under their own name. Buy the current year's lot and use it within the year; greens stale faster than the island's black teas.

Not the green tea to start with if you are new to green tea, but a very good one for Moroccan-style mint tea.
history:
Green tea on the island goes back to experiments with Chinese seedlings in the nineteenth century. As an export it is much newer, with the first batch dated to 1982 by the state's export board.

The same board lists Chun Mee, Sowmee, rolled gunpowder in grades GP1, GP2 and Special, and green fannings, and names the USA, Australia and Russia as the main markets. Export volumes are thin in print.
